issues.legal_issue: A law governing evacuee property that authorizes classification and supplies criteria for declaring property evacuee property is protected from a constitutional compensation challenge.
material_facts: The petitioner purchased land from a person later declared an intending evacuee who subsequently left India for Pakistan.
An official declared the purchased land to be evacuee property under a law governing evacuee property.
The petitioner challenged the law’s definition of evacuee property and its provisions for confirmation of transactions as permitting property to be taken without compensation.
issues.conclusion: The challenged provisions were not affected by the constitutional compensation requirement because the constitutional protection extends to laws that empower an authority to declare property evacuee property and lay down criteria for that determination.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(5)(b)(iii) protects provisions of laws made in pursuance of an agreement with another country or otherwise with respect to property declared by law to be evacuee property. That protection extends beyond laws that themselves identify particular property: it includes laws that authorize declarations and establish criteria for deciding what property may be declared evacuee property. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_property_classification and law_concerns_evacuee_property and law_authorizes_classification and law_sets_classification_criteria

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_cla: A person challenges the law used to classify property as evacuee property.
predicates.law_concerns_evacuee_property: The law concerns the treatment or classification of property as evacuee property.
predicates.law_authorizes_classification: The law empowers an authority to decide whether property is evacuee property.
predicates.law_sets_classification_criteria: The law supplies criteria for deciding whether property may be classified as evacuee property.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a law governing evacuee property that authorizes classification and provides criteria for it, the law is not invalidated by the compensation requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A deprivation resulting from a property declaration made under a valid law is not a deprivation without authority of law.
material_facts: The petitioner argued that declaring his purchased land to be evacuee property deprived him of property without authority of law.
The declaration was made under a law enacted by Parliament, and the Court rejected the constitutional challenge to the relevant provisions.
issues.conclusion: The declaration did not violate the prohibition on deprivation of property without authority of law because it was made pursuant to a law enacted by Parliament.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(1) prohibits deprivation of property save by authority of law. A deprivation resulting from a declaration made pursuant to a valid law enacted by Parliament is made under authority of law; the result would differ if the law were unconstitutional. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_dep: A person raises a constitutional challenge to being deprived of property.
predicates.deprivation_follows_official_property_de: An official declaration results in the person losing the property or its recognized status.
predicates.declaration_is_pursuant_to_valid_law: The official makes the declaration under a law that is valid.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns deprivation resulting from an official declaration made under a valid law, the deprivation satisfies the authority-of-law requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A power to refuse confirmation of a transaction for lack of good faith is not unconstitutional merely because the law does not prescribe a separate standard for determining good faith.
material_facts: The petitioner applied for confirmation of his purchase of land from an evacuee.
The Custodian rejected the application after finding that the evacuee had not acted in good faith in making the sale.
The petitioner argued that good faith was vague and that the Custodian therefore had arbitrary power.
issues.conclusion: The power to refuse confirmation on the ground that the transaction was not entered into in good faith was not unconstitutional for lack of a prescribed standard, because the power was judicial in nature.
issues.legal_principle: Section 40(4)(a) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, permits refusal to confirm a transaction that was not entered into in good faith. The Court observed that good faith has acquired a definite meaning in courts of law and held that the power was judicial in nature, so the absence of a separate standard did not render the provision unconstitutional. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_confirmation: A person constitutionally challenges an official decision on an application to confirm a transaction involving evacuee property.
predicates.confirmation_application_was_rejected_fo: The official refused confirmation because the transferor did not act in good faith when making the transaction.
predicates.decision_power_is_judicial: The official exercises the power through an inquiry and a decision of a judicial nature.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns refusal to confirm a transaction for the transferor’s lack of good faith and the decision power is judicial, the power is not unconstitutional merely for lacking a separate prescribed standard.

issues.legal_issue: A different outcome in another adjudication does not by itself establish discrimination when the challenged decision is judicial.
material_facts: The petitioner asserted that another sale by the same evacuee had been confirmed despite allegedly inadequate consideration, while his sale had adequate consideration but was not confirmed.
The petitioner’s sale was refused confirmation on the ground that the evacuee had not acted in good faith.
The Court characterized the Custodian’s decision as a judicial order and held that a possible error in another case did not establish discrimination against the petitioner.
issues.conclusion: The petitioner had not established discrimination merely by pointing to a different outcome in another case that the Custodian may have decided wrongly.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the Custodian’s confirmation decision as judicial and held that a possible error in another case does not, without more, establish discriminatory treatment. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.constitutional_petition_alleges_discrimi: A person alleges in a constitutional petition that an adjudicative decision treated them discriminatorily.
predicates.comparable_case_received_different_outco: A different transaction or case received an outcome more favorable to another person.
predicates.challenged_decision_is_judicial: The challenged official decision is judicial in nature.

issues.definition: When a constitutional petition relies on a different outcome in a comparable case to challenge a judicial decision, the different outcome alone does not establish discrimination.
